heading: Part 1: Welcome
teacher: Welcome to today's walk through an Italian market. You already met numbers up to twenty in the foundations course, and today they go to work. In the next ten minutes you will buy fruit by the kilo, ask prices, and order politely, all by recombining a handful of blocks.

heading: Part 2: Numbers framing
teacher: First, a quick recap. One to ten in Italian. You know these cold, and everything today is priced and weighed with them. Listen once to lock them in.

target.text: Uno, due, tre, quattro, cinque, sei, sette, otto, nove, dieci.
target.meaning: One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten.

heading: Part 3: Numbers teens
teacher: Now eleven to twenty. They stack onto ten the way English stacks teens. Notice seventeen and nineteen keep their full shape. Listen, because in two minutes these become prices.

target.text: Undici, dodici, tredici, quattordici, quindici, sedici, diciassette, diciotto, diciannove, venti.
target.meaning: Eleven, twelve, thirteen, fourteen, fifteen, sixteen, seventeen, eighteen, nineteen, twenty.

heading: Part 4: Think number
teacher: Quick check before we move on. Seventeen. You heard it buried in the list. Say it in your head right now. Ten seconds, then listen to confirm.

heading: Part 5: Un una
teacher: At an Italian market you buy quantities, not pieces. Two tiny words do the heavy lifting: a feminine word pairs with one of them, a masculine word with the other. Listen to how a kilo of apples is ordered.

heading: Part 6: Etto
teacher: Next block: short for one hundred grams. Cold cuts and cheese sell by it. A hundred grams of ham. Listen to the pattern with apples, then ham.

target.text: Un etto di prosciutto. Una fetta di formaggio.
target.meaning: A hundred grams of ham. A slice of cheese.

heading: Part 7: Costa think
teacher: Now prices. How much does it cost, for one thing. Think. You are at the stall with one melon in your hand. Build the question yourself, then take ten seconds and say it in your head. Then listen to the reveal.

heading: Part 8: Costano think
teacher: Many things change exactly one word: it gains an n, meaning they cost. Think. A pile of peaches catches your eye. Ask the vendor their price, then listen.

heading: Part 9: Prices
teacher: Answers come back as numbers you already own. Listen and count with the vendor: three euros, that is four euros, five euros and fifty cents.

target.text: Tre euro. Sono quattro euro. Cinque euro e cinquanta.
target.meaning: Three euros. That is four euros. Five euros and fifty cents.

heading: Part 10: Vorrei
teacher: Now the politest verb in the market: I would like, softer than I want. Please opens every request, and thanks closes it. Listen to a full request.

target.text: Due etti di prosciutto, per favore.
target.meaning: Two hundred grams of ham, please.

heading: Part 11: Courtesy
teacher: Markets run on greetings: good morning, many thanks, goodbye, until tomorrow. Listen to each.

target.text: Buongiorno, grazie mille! Arrivederci, a domani!
target.meaning: Good morning, thanks a lot! Goodbye, see you tomorrow!

heading: Part 12: Dialogue setup
teacher: Time to put it together. A customer, Elena, at a fruit stall. She greets, the vendor answers, she orders a kilo of apples, and asks the price of the grapes. Listen to the whole exchange.

target.text: Buongiorno! Vorrei un chilo di mele, per favore. Buongiorno! Mi dica pure. Quanto costano le pesche? Grazie mille, arrivederci!
target.meaning: Good morning! I would like a kilo of apples, please. Good morning! Go ahead, tell me. How much are the peaches? Thanks a lot, goodbye!

heading: Part 13: Challenge elena
teacher: Now you are Elena. The vendor greets you. You want three apples. Build the polite request, then the grapes catch your eye: one kilo, so the singular question. Ten seconds for both lines, in your head, then listen.

target.text: Vorrei tre mele, per favore. Quanto costa un chilo di uva?
target.meaning: I would like three apples, please. How much is a kilo of grapes?

heading: Part 14: Stall2 setup
teacher: One more stall, cheese this time, and the vendor answers back. Two new half-blocks: a price sentence that needs no verb phrase of its own, and a short word that takes the feminine thing, while masculine things take another form. Listen to the whole exchange: question, price, deal.

target.text: Quanto costa una fetta di formaggio? Costa due euro. La prendo, grazie.
target.meaning: How much is a slice of cheese? It costs two euros. I will take it, thanks.

heading: Part 15: Final think
teacher: Final challenge, and nobody taught you this one. You are back at the fruit stall. One melon, masculine. Ask its price, singular, then take it, masculine. Twelve seconds, in your head, then listen.

heading: Part 16: Final take think
teacher: He names the price. Now close the deal. The melon is masculine, so the short word is the masculine one. Listen.

heading: Part 17: Review pere think
teacher: One more review, mixing every block. Pears are feminine plural, and you want one kilo, so the masculine quantity word is right. A polite request, twelve seconds, in your head, then listen.

target.text: Vorrei un chilo di pere, per favore.
target.meaning: I would like a kilo of pears, please.

heading: Part 18: Closing
teacher: And that is the market. Gender picks the little word for a and one. Kilo and hundred grams weigh it. One thing or many things changes the price verb. Please and thank you wrap every request in politeness, and the verb for taking closes the deal. A handful of blocks, and you derived every sentence today, including ones nobody taught you.
